When working on worn or lightly damaged serials in a fully-legal, licensed gunsmithing or armorer setting, professionals will typically choose one of these five methods—always after verifying ATF/Federal and state requirements, getting any required approvals, and documenting every step:

1. Manual Stamp-and-Punch (“Hand Stamping”)  
   • Uses hardened-steel number punches and either a light bench hammer or small arbor press.  
   • Pros: Low cost, portable, works on most receiver steels.  
   • Cons: Depth and alignment depend on operator skill; can distort soft metals if overdriven.  
   • Best for: Simple restorations where only minor sharpening of existing digits is needed.

2. Arbor or Hydraulic Press Stamping  
   • Utilizes the same hardened-steel punches but driven by a calibrated arbor press or small hydraulic die-set.  
   • Pros: Very consistent depth and crispness, reduced risk of punch “walking,” faster than hand hammering.  
   • Cons: Requires dedicated equipment, careful fixturing to maintain original font spacing.  
   • Best for: Batch refinishing where uniformity is critical and multiple parts share the same serial.

3. CNC-Controlled Dot-Peen (Micro-Peen) Marking  
   • A computer‐controlled carbide stylus “dots” the characters into the metal in a precise grid pattern.  
   • Pros: Pixel-perfect spacing, programmable depth, very repeatable. Can mimic old-style fonts if desired.  
   • Cons: Slightly pebbly finish (not “solid” stamping), equipment cost.  
   • Best for: Curved surfaces, tight tolerances and whenever exact reproducibility is required.

4. Laser Engraving/Marking  
   • Fiber or diode lasers remove metal or change surface color to outline each digit.  
   • Pros: Extremely fine detail, no tooling wear, minimal mechanical stress, very fast.  
   • Cons: Initial capital outlay, needs proper fume extraction, depth control can be trickier in very hard steels.  
   • Best for: High-end restorations, small or hard-to-reach serial locations, or matching factory-style engraving.

5. Chemical or Electrochemical Etching (and Photo-Chemical Machining)  
   • A stencil or photo-resist mask is applied over the clean metal; acid or an electrolytic process lightly “bites” the exposed areas.  
   • Pros: No physical deformation, very uniform shallow etch, great on thin-walled or fragile parts.  
   • Cons: Requires precise masking, bath disposal considerations, limited to shallow depths.  
   • Best for: Thin receivers, magazine wells, or where stamping marks would be too aggressive.

Key compliance reminders for every method:  
• Always document the before/after condition with high-resolution photos.  
• Retain cut-sheet records of punches/laser settings or dot-peen files.  
• Secure written ATF approval (or follow your country’s equivalent) before re-serializing or deepening an obliterated number.  
• Ensure any new marking exactly matches the original font style, size and placement so as not to mislead or run afoul of “misbranding” rules.
